survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper does not conduct student-level ILSA microdata estimation with survey-weighted regression/ML. Instead, it uses (i) a text-analysis dataset of Facebook posts from US political party accounts and (ii) OECD-reported adult skill trends from the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) as descriptive evidence of changes in literacy and numeracy across countries. Because the analysis is not an ILSA microdata model with plausible-value achievement outcomes, there is no documented application of PIAAC sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGT or replicate weights) in the manuscript. For the PIAAC component, the authors rely on OECD-published country-level score changes and do not describe any student-level filtering, PV recombination, or complex-survey variance estimation steps.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not estimate a PV-based cognitive achievement model from ILSA microdata. The empirical components are (a) readability/complexity measures computed from social-media text and (b) OECD-published PIAAC country-level trends in literacy and numeracy, which are not analyzed as PV-based student achievement outcomes in the paper. As a result, plausible-value handling and a student-level missing-data strategy are not applicable to the reported analyses, and the manuscript does not document a missing-data procedure for microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: For the social-media component, the authors analyze Facebook posts from the Democratic Party (DNC) page and the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) page, excluding URLs/links and computing within-month dispersion of Dale–Chall readability scores across posts from each page since inception. For the PIAAC component, the authors use OECD-reported adult skills trends (literacy and numeracy) and report statistically significant changes between 2012–2022 at the 5% level; they explicitly drop Switzerland, Croatia, Latvia, and Portugal from the change analysis because they were not included in the first round and thus changes cannot be computed. No student-level inclusion/exclusion rules, PV recombination steps, or microdata filtering criteria are described because the paper relies on OECD-published country-level results.

Empirically, it provides suggestive evidence using (1) a text-analysis of Facebook posts from US political party accounts, where it computes the dispersion of Dale–Chall readability (a proxy for linguistic complexity) within months and finds statistically significant increasing trends in variance over time (with bootstrapped standard errors; point estimates around 0.13 for Democrats and 0.12 for Republicans). It also reports OECD PIAAC adult skills trends, describing declines in literacy and numeracy across most countries between 2012 and 2022, with a notable literacy decline in many settings (e.g., large negative changes for several countries). The evidence is descriptive and not a student-level, PV-based predictive ML analysis; therefore, no ML performance metrics, PV handling, or survey-weighted estimation details are provided, and causal identification is not established. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a theory-and-evidence paper rather than an empirical predictive ML study on ILSA microdata. The manuscript does not train or evaluate any machine-learning model, does not report PV-based achievement prediction metrics, and does not provide student-level sample sizes or survey-weighting variables. Consequently, fields required for ML predictive pipelines (ml_techniques, main_findings with target-variable prediction metrics, and confounder lists tied to ML features) are necessarily empty.
